transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-10-16 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Silva (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (VaporStack), Diego Morales (VaporStack), Emily Zhou (VaporStack procurement)
Links mentioned: https://redwood.ai/partner-deck v1, https://drive.redwood/ps/pilot-routing-matrix.xlsx (shared), security-scan-summary.pdf (to follow)

Summary (auto): Quick partner intro, high level onramp patterns, agreement to run a pilot focusing on hybrid routing + KV cache behavior.

00:00 Lena: hey everyone thanks for joining, um uh we're excited to meet the VaporStack team, i'm lena from redwood, i'll kick things off with a 5 minute overview and then marco will jump into the infra questions
00:15 Aisha: morning lena, thanks, excited to connect. quick context, vaporstack runs a mix of colocation and edge pop infrastructure, we do managed orchestration for telco and cloud native customers, we've had interest on two things, one is routing into customer VPCs and two is consistent GPU performance across our fleet
00:38 Marco: cool, can i ask about the profile of the models you're expecting, like seq lens, typical batch sizes, anything you can share will help, also are you thinking hosted endpoints or a private onramp model?
00:52 Diego: mostly seq lengths under 1024, a bunch of 512 workloads for summarization and some 2k-ish for retrieval augmented generation, batch sizes vary but we prefer low latency single requests, so batching is minimal, we are evaluating both a dedicated private onramp and a hybrid routing model where traffic can go to redwood hosted or to our on-prem pool depending on locality and cost
01:18 Lena: makes sense — that's the exact mix we see from customers that want predictable p99 but low unit cost. a couple of things we'll need to verify: network egress constraints, whether you can do VPC peering or need a VPN/CPE, and also key management for any customer data if they require KMS/HSM integration
01:39 Aisha: right, and security is important to our customers, most ask for SOC2 and an attestation, then usually SAML SSO for the console. procurement will want audit log access and longer retention for logs
01:58 Emily: yeah procurement here, key questions for us are pricing bands for hybrid routing, minimum commit for dedicated pools, and what the SLAs look like for failover to hosted when our on-prem is degraded
02:15 Marco: perfect i'll take the SLA and failover details offline with the team, redwood supports automatic fallback to compatible model variants — that may help with graceful degradation. on the security side we have SOC2 and can provide the summary report, for KMS we support external KMS via customer-managed keys
02:39 Aisha: quick clarifying question — when you say fallback to variant do you mean a smaller quantized model or a different architecture?
02:47 Marco: usually a compatible quantized variant, same architecture family, it's meant to keep latency low while preserving output stability; there are some tradeoffs in top-k sampling and occasional tokenization differences but we run eval sets to ensure quality thresholds
03:10 Diego: so about routing, are you able to do per-tenant routing rules? we have a flow where some customers must stay on-prem for data residency, others can burst to hosted to save cost
03:25 Lena: yes, we support policy-based routing — you can set by tenant, region, or cost tier. we also do automatic KV caching and prefix caching which reduces token costs for repetitive prompts. marco can talk specifics about the KV cache sizing and eviction policies
03:44 Marco: yeah the KV cache is a working-set cache that keeps recent KV shards in GPU memory when possible; there are eviction policies based on recency and token counts. note: in some transcribes the system transcribed KV cache as KV cash which is meh — sorry for that transcript noise
04:01 Aisha: ha yeah i've seen that before, ok practical question: network roundtrip — if we do VPC peering to redwood hosted endpoints, what's a realistic tail latency for 512 tokens?
04:16 Marco: with our optimized kernels and batching it's common to see p50 under 40ms for small models, p95 depends on tail traffic and network hop — for hosted-to-hosted in-region we often hit p95 ~120-150ms for the model mix you described; with on-prem local serving you'll see much lower network latency but need to provision GPUs to hit p99 targets
04:42 Diego: what about quantization? some of our fleet uses 8-bit quantized models for cost — does that change behavior dramatically for generation latency or correctness?
04:54 Marco: quantization reduces memory and often improves throughput but there are accuracy tradeoffs on some tasks; we provide recommended quant profiles per model and run regression tests. in many cases 4-bit and 8-bit profiles are supported with small output diffs; we'll share our quant table in the partner deck
05:12 Emily: procurement aside — we'd like to see an indicative pilot price, even a ballpark, to go to budget owners
05:21 Lena: we can do banded pilots — small POC under $XXk, or a 6-week hybrid pilot priced based on reserved GPU hours plus a small integration fee, i'll put a draft SOW in the next steps
05:36 Diego: on the technical side, what's your recommended connectivity for our edge pops, do you recommend dedicated peering per region or a centralized hub?
05:47 Marco: depends on traffic patterns; for low RTT it's best to peer regionally near the edge pop; if you prefer simplified management, hub-and-spoke with regional egress nodes is fine but adds a hop. Also we need to account for TLS termination and HSM proxied calls if you're using customer keys
06:12 Aisha: regarding keys: we want to keep keys in our KMS, so is there an option to proxy KMS calls or have HSM-backed signing in our environment?
06:23 Marco: yes we support customer-managed keys and can either proxy KMS calls or host a key-vault connector in your VPC; if the pilot requires air-gapped HSM we can discuss an on-prem package but that raises integration time and cost
06:42 Diego: fine. any constraints about GPU drivers or CUDA versions for your on-prem package? we run a mixed fleet with 5300 and 7400 series equivalents
06:54 Marco: we publish compatible driver matrix; typical constraints are kernel-level drivers and a minimum CUDA 12.x for some of our optimized kernels; we also provide container images tuned per GPU family. we'll share the compatibility matrix in the tech deep-dive doc
07:18 Lena: shifting to success criteria — what's a win for VaporStack after the pilot?
07:25 Aisha: win is defined as 20-30% lower per-token cost for burst traffic, consistent p99 below 350ms for our critical customers, and a validated routing policy that keeps sensitive tenants on-prem with zero egress leakage
07:44 Marco: good measurable goals. we'll propose bench targets that align — we'll test p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1M tokens for your mix. one note: caching can drastically lower cost on repetitive prompts, but must be validated per customer to ensure correctness
08:09 Diego: ok about data residency — are there audit logs and S3 access logs available for per-request tracing? customers will want request-level telemetry for compliance
08:21 Marco: yes we stream audit logs to customer-owned storage or to our console export; we support extended retention for enterprise add-ons. logs include request headers, model version, latency, and trace ids but we can redact payloads on request
08:41 Emily: that sounds promising. procurement question — is there a standard enterprise addendum for liability and data protections?
08:49 Lena: yes we have standard EAA language, and for larger deals we customize indemnity and data processing addenda. we'll push a sample EA to you in the drive
09:02 Aisha: switching gear — curious about orchestration: how does autoscaling work if we have bursty traffic from on-prem to hosted? is there a cold-start problem?
09:15 Marco: our autoscaler uses continuous batching and keeps warm pools for common model families; cold-starts are rare for commonly-used models, but for long-tail custom models you may see cold-starts. for hybrid we recommend a minimal reserved capacity plus a burst policy to hosted with scaled concurrency limits to avoid cold starts causing tail spikes
09:44 Diego: makes sense. any differences if we use VPC peering versus VPN overlay? we have some customers who restrict BGP peering
09:54 Marco: peering is lower latency and preferred; VPN overlay works but add a NAT/translation hop and can add jitter. either is fine for pilot but for production at scale peering is recommended
10:10 Aisha: we talked to a competitor (NimbusGrid) and they had a different approach to KV caching, they wanted to push caching to edge nodes — are you compatible with edge-first caching?
10:23 Marco: we can support edge caching for prefixes, it's a topology choice. Redwood's runtime supports multi-level caches — local GPU KV, regional cache, and host-level caches — coordination is handled in the routing layer. there can be consistency implications for session-based generation
10:47 Diego: ok let's talk integration points briefly, what artifacts do you need from us to spin a pilot?
10:55 Lena: network topology, firewall/IP allowlist, SSO metadata for SAML, KMS access pattern, and an initial sample dataset or eval prompts to run regression tests. also a contact person for network ops and one for security
11:12 Aisha: we'll compile those and share, can you confirm expected lead time once we hand over artifacts?
11:20 Marco: typical onboarding for a hybrid pilot is 2-3 weeks for basic peering and test harness; if HSM/on-prem package is involved it's more like 6-8 weeks. depends on approvals and firewall windows
11:43 Emily: procurement will need invoice terms — are you able to do net-30?
11:49 Lena: standard is net-30 for pilots; for dedicated reserved capacity usually net-45 or negotiated for larger customers but we'll put payment terms in the SOW
12:05 Diego: curious about profiling — can you run our internal microbenchmarks? we have a small harness that runs concurrent inference across 16 GPUs, can your SE team run that or do we run and share results?
12:20 Marco: we can run partner microbenchmarks in our test cluster or you can run in your environment with our tooling. for fairness we prefer to run mirrored tests in both infra profiles and compare traces
12:37 Aisha: ok, helps. any blockers you foresee?
12:42 Marco: the usual blockers are firewall windows and KMS approvals. also if your fleet uses older CUDA versions we'll need driver updates which can be scheduling sensitive
12:58 Diego: noted. quick question on metrics — do you provide token-level cost breakdown by route? we need to show internal customers where cost delta comes from
13:10 Marco: yes our console has per-route and per-model breakdowns, token-level cost, and cost attribution per tenant; we can provide a limited-access demo to your finance folks in the pilot
13:28 Lena: ok we're nearing the end of our agenda. to recap: we'll send security artifacts, partner deck, and a draft SOW; marco will run bench and share results; vaporstack will provide network topology and eval prompts. anything we missed?
13:45 Aisha: timeline looks good, we'll aim to have artifacts to you by monday 2029-10-21, procurement will review SOW and come back with a PO if numbers align
13:58 Emily: yep procurement will aim for internal approval within two weeks of receiving pilot SOW
14:08 Diego: technical deep-dive preferred week of 10/22, marco let me know availability
14:15 Marco: i'll send calendar invites, i'm available mornings PST that week
14:24 Lena: thanks everyone, we'll share links and next steps after the call. action items in the calendar invite. bye
14:32 Aisha: thanks lena, bye
